doc.title: Tony Marino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 25, 2025

title: Liebman's Coltrane tributes and older masters
summary: Coltrane's Meditation tributes with Reggie Workman, Cecil McBee, Billy Hart and Sonny Fortune; stories from Clark Terry; welcome from older Black musicians.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I think you were involved with Dave in Coltrane tributes?

Yeah he did “Coltrane’s Meditation” it was every five years he would do it. And I got to do a few of them. I got to do them in Europe and I got to play double bass with Reggie Workman for instance. The one we recorded was with Cecil McBee. I did it once in the Water Gap with Michael Formanek that both of us played. So there were a few episodes of that he would do you know, and his wife Caris wrote/transcribed the melodies and so we had that form to pull out. I remember when we played with – it was Reggie Workman, and Billy Hart with the other drummer Jamey Haddad. There was two drummers, two bass players. And Sonny Fortune I remember. And the next day we were at breakfast and I’m sitting there and Reggie Workman comes in and I was thrilled to be sitting with him and Sonny Fortune. “Coltrane didn’t write that shit out. You know? He didn’t write any of that out.” He was upset that there was written music. But I took care of that. You know he didn’t have to. I just let him go and do what he does you know. And I took care of the mopping up the floor and, you know. So but it was a great experience and in Europe too where it works there. And it works in New York too, not everywhere but.
Rubbing elbows with those gentlemen from the earlier era is so enriching.

Yeah. Oh it is. You get on a bus and some of these greats come and they start talking stories and I mean it’s just – you realize they’re human and it’s so great to, you know, experience what they experienced you know. But you know when you think about the older black musicians with the racial thing they had to go through, I don’t have a clue. What that was, I’ll never know what that is. You know but they never – I mean my experience is I didn’t feel ever that racial thing with them. They always made me feel welcome into the music you know. And Clark Terry – he was a great storyteller. We were on the bus once you know and Lieb was a really good – he’d be a good emcee on a talk show, because he would ask the questions to get him going. And it was really fun on that bus ride to the venue to be with Clark Terry and hear his stories, Miles’ drug addiction or whatever. It was great to be – what a great spirit man. Wow.
I was able to have some of that spirit next to me in this project I do, so I know what you’re talking about.
Yeah. They lived a special life you know. And we try to make ‘em proud, hopefully.
